subject: Computer Networking
title: Interference and Noise
description: A fast breakdown of Interference and Noise for builders.

hook.text: Your Wi-Fi slows down when you microwave popcorn. Both devices fight over the same 2.4 GHz frequency.

buildup.text: Interference happens when multiple devices transmit on the same frequency. Signals collide and corrupt each other.

discovery.text: Spread spectrum techniques spread data across multiple frequencies. If one is noisy, others still get through.

twist.text: In dense apartments, dozens of Wi-Fi networks overlap on the same channels. Congestion, not distance, kills performance.

climax.text: The 5 GHz and 6 GHz bands have more channels. Less crowded means less interference and faster speeds.

punchline.text: Wireless isn't just about signal. It's about avoiding noise.

quiz.question: Why does the 5 GHz band often perform better than 2.4 GHz?
options: It has more channels and less interference from other devices
It has longer range than 2.4 GHz

details.summary: Wireless signals degrade from interference with other transmitters, physical obstacles, atmospheric conditions, and electronic noise. Co-channel interference occurs when devices share frequencies, while multipath interference happens when reflected signals arrive at different times.
details.whyItMatters: Interference is the primary limit on wireless network performance. Understanding its sources and solutions explains why Wi-Fi slows down in crowded areas and what engineers can do about it.
takeaways: Co-channel interference occurs when nearby devices share frequencies
Multipath reflections cause signals to arrive out of phase
Signal-to-noise ratio determines achievable data rates

faq.question: Why does Wi-Fi slow down in crowded places?
faq.answer: Many devices sharing the same frequency channels cause co-channel interference. Each device must wait its turn to transmit, reducing individual throughput. Neighboring networks on the same channel add noise.

faq.question: What is the signal-to-noise ratio?
faq.answer: SNR measures the difference between signal strength and background noise in decibels. Higher SNR means cleaner signals and faster data rates. Below a threshold, the receiver cannot decode data reliably.
